# Factors, Strings, and Dates {#sec-types}

```{r}
#| label: types-opening
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
hf_dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw_data", "hfhome")
opening_meds <- read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, "medications.csv"),
                         col_types = cols(.default = col_character()))
opening_match <- str_match(
  opening_meds$med_text,
  regex(paste0("(\\d+(?:\\.\\d+)?)(?:\\s*[/-]\\s*\\d+(?:\\.\\d+)?)?",
               "\\s*(mg|mcg|meq|units)\\b"), ignore_case = TRUE)
)
opening_unit <- str_to_lower(opening_match[, 3])
opening_mg <- case_when(
  opening_unit == "mg" ~ as.numeric(opening_match[, 2]),
  opening_unit == "mcg" ~ as.numeric(opening_match[, 2]) / 1000
)
opening_naive <- as.numeric(str_extract(opening_meds$med_text, "\\d+"))
opening_n <- sum(!is.na(opening_mg))
opening_wrong <- sum(opening_naive != opening_mg, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Numeric columns misbehave loudly: a value that should be a number
and is not stops the analysis within the minute. Text, categories,
and dates fail the other way. Take the first number in each HF-HOME
discharge medication string as its dose in milligrams, and
`r format(opening_wrong, big.mark = ",")` of the
`r format(opening_n, big.mark = ",")` doses written in milligrams
or micrograms are wrong, with no error: `Nitroglycerin 0.4 mg`
becomes 0 mg, and `digoxin 125 mcg` becomes 125 mg, a thousand
times the prescribed dose. A date parsed under the wrong convention
is still a date, and a factor with an unintended reference level
still fits a model. Each produces a result rather than an error,
and the result looks exactly as it should; this chapter makes each
of those failures loud.

::: {.bookepigraph}

```{=latex}
\begin{flushright}\small
```

invalidation and naming things.*

```{=latex}

```
:::

## Factors: categories with a declared level set {#sec-types-factors}

A character vector is flexible: any value, any order, any new value
later. A factor is constrained: a fixed set of levels, a defined
order, and a first level that a model treats as the reference. For
analysis the constraints are correct, because the model needs the
level set and the reference. For cleaning and joining they are a
hazard, because a new or misspelled value has nowhere to go. The
decision is therefore not whether to use factors but *when* to
convert, and @fig-factor-timing gives the answer this chapter
argues for (Habit 7).

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-factor-timing
%%| fig-alt: "Left-to-right chain. Read, clean and recode, and join
%%|   all stay in character type. A highlighted node marks where to
%%|   convert to factor, setting the reference level deliberately.
%%|   From there the chain branches to Model and to Plot, both
%%|   working in factor type."
%%| fig-cap: "Where to convert. Character is the safe type through
%%|   reading, cleaning, and joining, because a new or misspelled
%%|   value is merely a new string rather than an invalid level.
%%|   Factor is the correct type at modeling and plotting, because
%%|   the model needs a fixed level set and a declared reference."
flowchart LR
  R["Read<br/><i>character</i>"] --> C["Clean and recode<br/><i>character</i>"]
  C --> J["Join<br/><i>character</i>"]
  J --> X["<b>Convert here</b><br/><i>factor, reference level<br/>set deliberately</i>"]
  X --> M["Model<br/><i>factor</i>"]
  X --> P["Plot<br/><i>factor, ordered<br/>by fct_reorder</i>"]
```

The generic tour of `forcats` is in R for Data Science
[@wickham2023r4ds, ch. 16], and the full verb list is in the cheat
sheet at the end of this chapter. The sections below start from a
problem in the HF-HOME export and reach for the verb that solves
it.

### A variable coded four ways

The case report form (CRF) export records sex as `F`/`M` at two sites, `Female`/`Male`
at one, `f`/`m` at another, and `2`/`1` at Site D, whose codebook
maps 1 to male and 2 to female. @sec-wrangling recoded these with
`case_when()`; `forcats::fct_collapse()` does the same in the
vocabulary of levels:

```{r}
#| label: types-sex
library(tidyverse)
hf_dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw_data", "hfhome")

crf_raw <- read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, "crf_export.csv"),
                    col_types = cols(.default = col_character()),
                    na = character()) |>
  mutate(site_raw = site,
         site = str_to_title(str_squish(site)),
         patient_id = str_pad(patient_id, width = 4, pad = "0"))

crf_typed <- crf_raw |>
  mutate(sex = fct_collapse(sex,
                            F = c("F", "Female", "f", "2"),
                            M = c("M", "Male", "m", "1")) |>
           fct_relevel("F", "M"))
levels(crf_typed$sex)
crf_typed |> count(site, raw = crf_raw$sex, sex)
```

The collapsed levels come out in the order of the raw codes they
absorbed, so `fct_relevel()` states the order you want. More
important, `fct_collapse()` leaves any code you did not list as a
level of its own, without a warning. That is why the levels are
printed, and why the verification below asserts them: an unexpected
code, such as `U` arriving next quarter, then stops the script
instead of becoming a third sex.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
The running study ships the clean `demographics.csv`, so the recode
can be checked against an answer key:

```{r}
#| label: types-sex-verify
demographics <- read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, "demographics.csv"),
                         col_types = cols(patient_id = col_character()),
                         show_col_types = FALSE)
key <- match(crf_typed$patient_id, demographics$patient_id)

stopifnot(
  identical(levels(crf_typed$sex), c("F", "M")),
  !anyNA(key),
  all(as.character(crf_typed$sex) == demographics$sex[key])
)
```

A real export has no answer key; there, the cross-tabulation above,
read line by line against each site's codebook, is the check.
:::

### Declaring the level set

The site labels arrive in fifteen spellings of five sites. A factor
built with `factor()` and no levels accepts all fifteen, in
alphabetical order. A factor built with the levels the protocol
names turns every other spelling into `NA`, which an assertion can
catch:

```{r}
#| label: types-site
site_levels <- paste("Site", LETTERS[1:5])

nlevels(factor(crf_raw$site_raw))

crf_typed <- crf_typed |>
  mutate(site = factor(site, levels = site_levels))
stopifnot(!anyNA(crf_typed$site))
fct_count(crf_typed$site)
```

Declared levels also fix the order of every table and figure. Use
`fct_infreq()` or `fct_reorder()` when the order should follow the
data, as in a bar chart sorted by count; keep the protocol's order
when the reader will look for a site by name.

### The reference level

`randomization.csv` records the arm as `Usual care` or
`Home health`. Left to `factor()`, the levels are alphabetical, so
`Home health` becomes the reference and the model reports the effect
of usual care:

```{r}
#| label: types-reference
randomization <- read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, "randomization.csv"),
                          col_types = cols(.default = col_character()))
outcomes <- read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, "outcomes.csv"),
                     col_types = cols(patient_id = col_character()),
                     show_col_types = FALSE)
trial <- randomization |>
  inner_join(outcomes, by = "patient_id",
             relationship = "one-to-one")

levels(factor(trial$arm))

fit_default <- glm(event_30d ~ arm, family = binomial,
                   data = trial |> mutate(arm = factor(arm)))
fit_declared <- glm(event_30d ~ arm, family = binomial,
                    data = trial |> mutate(arm = factor(
                      arm, levels = c("Usual care", "Home health"))))
coef(fit_default)[2]
coef(fit_declared)[2]
```

The two coefficients have the same size and opposite signs. Neither
is wrong; a reader who assumes the usual-care arm is the comparison
reads the first one's direction backwards. Declare the reference in
the cleaning script, in writing, where a reviewer can see it.
Whether the estimate is distinguishable from zero is a question for
the analysis plan (@sec-analysis-plan), not for the factor.

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
> **Context.** My model is `glm(event_30d ~ arm + site + sex,
> family = binomial)`. The levels of each factor, as printed by
> `levels()`, are below, with one sentence from the protocol naming
> the control arm.
>
> **Constraints.** Do not refit or change the formula. Set levels
> with `factor(..., levels = )` or `forcats::fct_relevel()` in the
> data-cleaning step, not inside the model call.
>
> **Criteria.** For each factor, say which level is the reference
> now, which it should be and why, and write the code that sets it.
> Then state in one sentence what the `arm` coefficient will mean
> after the change, including its sign convention.

*Failure mode.* Models assert that 'the first level is the
reference' without checking which level is first, or set the
reference inside the formula with `relevel()` where the next model
in the script does not inherit it. *Check.* Run `levels()` on each
factor after the change, refit, and confirm that the coefficient's
name (`armHome health`) names the treated arm. Send level names,
never rows (@sec-ai-governance).
:::

### Factors in joins and arithmetic

A `dplyr` join on factor keys compares labels, not the integer codes
behind them, so the rows match correctly. Two subtler things happen,
both without a warning:

```{r}
#| label: types-factor-join
a <- tibble(site = factor(c("Site A", "Site B")), x = 1:2)
b <- tibble(site = factor(c("Site B", "Site C")), y = 3:4)
joined <- full_join(a, b, by = "site")
levels(joined$site)
as.integer(a$site[a$site == "Site B"])
as.integer(b$site[b$site == "Site B"])

site_number <- factor(c("10", "2", "3"))
as.numeric(site_number)
as.numeric(as.character(site_number))
```

The joined key acquires the union of both level sets, in an order
neither table chose, and `Site B` is code 2 in one table and code 1
in the other.

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**`as.numeric()` on a factor returns its codes, not its labels.**
A site number stored as a factor, `10`, `2`, `3`, becomes 1, 2, 3,
because the codes follow the alphabetical order of the labels. Any
join or calculation on those codes pairs rows by position in the
level set, with the wrong labels and no error. Convert through
`as.character()`, or better, keep identifiers and numbers out of
factors altogether.
:::

### Exercises

1. Build `site` as a factor with the five protocol levels from the
   raw labels after `str_squish()` only, without `str_to_title()`.
   How many patients become `NA`, and under which raw spellings?
2. Fit `lm(event_30d ~ arm, data = trial)` with the default levels
   and with `fct_relevel(arm, "Usual care")`. Verify that the two
   `arm` coefficients are equal in size and opposite in sign, and
   say which one is the risk difference for home health against
   usual care.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-14-1
squished <- crf_raw |>
  mutate(site_f = factor(str_squish(site_raw), levels = site_levels))
sum(is.na(squished$site_f))
squished |>
  filter(is.na(site_f)) |>
  count(spelling = str_squish(site_raw))
```

Every upper- and lower-case variant is refused, which is the point
of declaring the levels: the `NA`s are a list of what the cleaning
step still has to handle. With `factor()` and no levels, each of
these spellings would have become a site of its own.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-14-2
lm_default <- lm(event_30d ~ arm, data = trial)
lm_declared <- lm(event_30d ~ arm,
                  data = trial |> mutate(arm = fct_relevel(arm,
                                                           "Usual care")))
stopifnot(all.equal(unname(coef(lm_default)[2]),
                    -unname(coef(lm_declared)[2])))
coef(lm_declared)[2]
```

With `Usual care` as the reference, the coefficient `armHome
health` is the difference in the proportion with an event, home
health minus usual care, among ascertained patients. A negative
value favors home health. The default model reports the same number
with the sign reversed, under the name `armUsual care`.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** This chapter keeps categorical variables as character
through reading, cleaning, and joining, and converts to factor only
for modeling and plotting. What goes wrong if you convert at read
time instead?

**Answer.** Recoding becomes harder: assigning a value that is not
already a level yields `NA` with a warning rather than the value you
assigned, and `str_replace()` on a factor silently returns
character. Joining becomes harder to reason about: two independently
built factors rarely share a level set, the joined key acquires the
union of both, and the codes behind the labels differ between
tables, which bites as soon as anyone calls `as.integer()` on a key.
A factor encodes a fixed set of categories and a reference level,
which is exactly what a model needs and exactly what makes it
brittle while the data are still moving.
:::

## Strings: structure from free text {#sec-types-strings}

`medications.csv` has one row per discharge medication, and its
`med_text` column records each as the prescriber typed it. The
`r format(nrow(opening_meds), big.mark = ",")` rows use
`r n_distinct(opening_meds$med_text)` distinct strings, mixing brand
and generic names, `mg` with and without a space, upper and lower
case, combination doses, units other than milligrams, and a dozen
ways to say how often. The generic tour of `stringr` and regular
expressions is in R for Data Science [@wickham2023r4ds, chs. 14 and
15]; this section answers three questions a statistician asks of
this column.

```{r}
#| label: types-meds-read
meds <- read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, "medications.csv"),
                 col_types = cols(patient_id = col_character(),
                                  med_seq = col_integer(),
                                  med_text = col_character()))
meds |> filter(patient_id == "0001") |> pull(med_text)
```

### Which drug?

How many discharge prescriptions are for furosemide? The obvious
pattern undercounts twice, once for case and once for the brand
name:

```{r}
#| label: types-detect
c(
  case_sensitive = sum(str_detect(meds$med_text, "furosemide")),
  ignore_case = sum(str_detect(meds$med_text,
                               regex("furosemide", ignore_case = TRUE))),
  with_brand = sum(str_detect(meds$med_text,
                              regex("furosemide|lasix",
                                    ignore_case = TRUE)))
)
```

Each count is a plausible number of prescriptions, and only the
last is right. A drug question therefore starts with a lookup that
names every spelling, brand and generic, for each class the
analysis needs. For a heart-failure trial, three classes matter
first: sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors, the
angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI)
sacubitril-valsartan, and loop diuretics.

```{r}
#| label: types-classes
meds <- meds |>
  mutate(drug_class = case_when(
    str_detect(med_text,
               regex("dapagliflozin|farxiga|empagliflozin|jardiance",
                     ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "SGLT2 inhibitor",
    str_detect(med_text, regex("sacubitril|entresto",
                               ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "ARNI",
    str_detect(med_text, regex("furosemide|lasix|torsemide",
                               ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Loop diuretic"
  ))
meds |>
  filter(!is.na(drug_class)) |>
  count(drug_class, med_text)
```

The cross-tabulation is the verification: every spelling that
matched is listed beside its class, so a reader can see that
`Farxiga` was counted and that nothing else was.

### What dose?

The dose is a number, possibly with a decimal point, possibly a
pair for a combination tablet (`49/51`, `24-26`), followed by a
unit. The pattern below captures each part with a group, and
`str_match()` returns one column per group:

```{r}
#| label: types-dose
dose_pattern <- regex(
  paste0("(\\d+(?:\\.\\d+)?)",
         "(?:\\s*[/-]\\s*(\\d+(?:\\.\\d+)?))?",
         "\\s*(mg|mcg|meq|units)\\b"),
  ignore_case = TRUE
)
dose_parts <- str_match(meds$med_text, dose_pattern)

meds <- meds |>
  mutate(
    dose    = as.numeric(dose_parts[, 2]),
    dose_2  = as.numeric(dose_parts[, 3]),
    unit    = str_to_lower(dose_parts[, 4]),
    dose_mg = case_when(unit == "mg" ~ dose,
                        unit == "mcg" ~ dose / 1000)
  )
meds |> count(unit)
meds |> filter(!is.na(dose_2)) |> count(med_text, dose, dose_2)
```

@tbl-regex-constructs reads the pattern piece by piece.

| Piece | Matches | Why it is there |
|---|---|---|
| `\\d+(?:\\.\\d+)?` | `40`, `0.4`, `12.5` | A dose with or without a decimal part; `(?: )` groups without capturing |
| `(?:\\s*[/-]\\s*(...))?` | `/51`, `-26`, or nothing | The second component of a combination tablet, captured separately |
| `\\s*` | Zero or more spaces | `40mg` and `40 mg` alike |
| `(mg\|mcg\|meq\|units)` | The unit | Requiring a unit stops `q5min` from being read as a dose |
| `\\b` | A word boundary | `mg` but not the start of a longer word |
| `ignore_case = TRUE` | `MG`, `mEq` | Prescribers' capitalization varies |

: The constructs in the dose pattern. In an R string each regular
expression backslash is written twice. {#tbl-regex-constructs}

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**A pattern that takes the first number misreads decimals, units,
and combination doses, and returns a number every time.**
`str_extract(x, "\\d+")` reads `0.4 mg` as 0, `12.5 mg` as 12, and
`digoxin 125 mcg` as 125, which a later step treats as milligrams.
`24-26 mg` is a combination tablet, 24 mg of sacubitril and 26 mg
of valsartan, not a range and not 24 mg. Require the unit in the
pattern, capture the decimal part, and convert units explicitly.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Every row should yield a dose and a unit from a known set, and two
spellings of the same prescription should agree once units are
converted:

```{r}
#| label: types-dose-verify
digoxin <- meds |>
  filter(str_detect(med_text, regex("digoxin", ignore_case = TRUE)))
stopifnot(
  !anyNA(meds$dose),
  setequal(unique(meds$unit), c("mg", "mcg", "meq", "units")),
  n_distinct(digoxin$dose_mg) == 1
)
digoxin |> count(med_text, dose_mg)
```

`0.125 mg` and `125 mcg` are the same dose, and the assertion says
so. A first-number parse fails this check by a factor of a thousand.
:::

### How often?

The frequency is written as Latin abbreviations with and without
periods (`BID`, `b.i.d.`), as English (`twice daily`,
`once a day`), and as timing (`QAM`, `qhs`, `at bedtime`). Remove
the periods and the case, then map each phrase to doses per day.
`PRN` (as needed) has no fixed daily count and stays `NA`.

```{r}
#| label: types-frequency
freq_pattern <- paste(
  "\\bprn\\b", "\\bbid\\b", "twice daily", "\\btid\\b", "\\bqd\\b",
  "once daily", "once a day", "every day", "daily", "\\bqam\\b",
  "\\bqhs\\b", "at bedtime", sep = "|"
)

meds <- meds |>
  mutate(
    freq_text = med_text |> str_to_lower() |> str_remove_all("\\."),
    freq_code = str_extract(freq_text, freq_pattern),
    per_day = case_when(
      freq_code == "prn" ~ NA_real_,
      freq_code %in% c("bid", "twice daily") ~ 2,
      freq_code == "tid" ~ 3,
      freq_code %in% c("qd", "once daily", "once a day", "every day",
                       "daily", "qam", "qhs", "at bedtime") ~ 1
    )
  )
meds |> count(per_day, freq_code)
```

Two details carry the weight. `str_extract()` returns the leftmost
match, so `twice daily` is found before the `daily` inside it; a
`case_when()` that tested `str_detect(x, "daily")` first would call
every twice-daily prescription once daily. And the word boundaries
in `\\bqd\\b` and `\\bbid\\b` keep the codes from matching inside
longer words.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Every row has a frequency code, and the only rows without a daily
count are the as-needed ones:

```{r}
#| label: types-frequency-verify
stopifnot(
  !anyNA(meds$freq_code),
  all(is.na(meds$per_day) == (meds$freq_code == "prn"))
)
```
:::

### Exercises

3. Count *patients*, not prescriptions, discharged on an SGLT2
   inhibitor in each arm. Join to `randomization.csv` with a
   declared relationship.
4. Compute the daily furosemide dose (`dose_mg * per_day`) for every
   furosemide prescription, in any spelling. Then recompute
   `per_day` with a `case_when()` that tests for `daily` before
   `twice daily`, and count the prescriptions, across all drugs,
   whose daily count changes.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-14-3
sglt2_patients <- meds |>
  filter(drug_class == "SGLT2 inhibitor") |>
  distinct(patient_id)

randomization |>
  left_join(sglt2_patients |> mutate(on_sglt2 = TRUE),
            by = "patient_id", relationship = "one-to-one") |>
  mutate(on_sglt2 = coalesce(on_sglt2, FALSE)) |>
  count(arm, on_sglt2) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n), .by = arm)
```

`distinct()` comes first because a patient could hold two SGLT2
prescriptions; without it the join would be one-to-many and the
declared relationship would refuse it. The shares in the two arms
are within a few percentage points of each other, as randomization
leads you to expect for a medication prescribed before the arm
could influence it; a large difference would be worth a data query.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-14-4
meds |>
  filter(str_detect(med_text, regex("furosemide|lasix",
                                    ignore_case = TRUE))) |>
  mutate(daily_mg = dose_mg * per_day) |>
  count(med_text, daily_mg)

wrong_order <- case_when(
  str_detect(meds$freq_text, "\\bprn\\b") ~ NA_real_,
  str_detect(meds$freq_text, "daily") ~ 1,
  str_detect(meds$freq_text, "\\bbid\\b|twice daily") ~ 2,
  str_detect(meds$freq_text, "\\btid\\b") ~ 3,
  str_detect(meds$freq_text,
             "\\bqd\\b|once a day|every day|\\bqam\\b|\\bqhs\\b|at bedtime") ~ 1
)
sum(wrong_order != meds$per_day, na.rm = TRUE)
meds |>
  filter(wrong_order != per_day) |>
  count(med_text)
```

Every `twice daily` prescription is halved, including the `Lasix
40 mg twice daily` rows, whose daily furosemide dose drops from 80
mg to 40 mg. No value is `NA` and no assertion on types fails;
only the cross-tabulation of codes against counts shows it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A colleague flags beta-blockers with
`str_detect(med_text, "olol")`, because their generic names end that
way. What does the flag count in this file, and what does it miss?

**Answer.** Tabulate it against the spellings you know to be
beta-blockers:

```{r}
#| label: types-olol
meds |>
  filter(str_detect(med_text, regex("olol|coreg|toprol",
                                    ignore_case = TRUE))) |>
  count(med_text, flagged = str_detect(med_text, "olol"))
```

The flag counts metoprolol written generically and misses
carvedilol, whose name ends in `-dilol`, and the brands `Coreg` and
`Toprol XL`. A suffix is a property of some names, not of the class.
Build class flags from a lookup that names each drug, brand and
generic, with `ignore_case = TRUE`, and print the matched spellings
beside the class, as in `types-classes`, so a reader can see what
was counted.
:::

## Dates: formats, ambiguity, and time {#sec-types-dates}

The CRF export writes dates in four formats: `YYYY-MM-DD` at Sites
A and B, `MM/DD/YYYY` at Site C, `DD-MON-YYYY` at Site D, and
`YYYYMMDD` at Site E. @sec-wrangling parsed them site by site, and
noted that a single call to `lubridate::parse_date_time()` with a
list of formats returns a date for every row and gets some of them
wrong. This section shows why, and how to find the rows at risk.
The generic tour is in R for Data Science [@wickham2023r4ds,
ch. 17].

### One parser, several formats

`parse_date_time()` accepts several `orders` and returns, for each
value, a date under one of them. The per-site parse uses one order
per site, as each site's codebook states:

```{r}
#| label: types-dates
parse_site_date <- function(x, site) {
  case_when(
    site %in% c("Site A", "Site B", "Site E") ~ ymd(x, quiet = TRUE),
    site == "Site C" ~ mdy(x, quiet = TRUE),
    site == "Site D" ~ dmy(x, quiet = TRUE)
  )
}

dates <- crf_raw |>
  transmute(
    site, discharge_raw = discharge_date,
    by_site = parse_site_date(discharge_date, site),
    one_call = as_date(parse_date_time(discharge_date,
                                       orders = c("ymd", "mdy", "dmy"),
                                       quiet = TRUE))
  )

dates |> count(site, wrong = by_site != one_call)
dates |> filter(by_site != one_call) |> distinct() |> head(4)

misread <- dates |>
  filter(by_site != one_call) |>
  summarize(n = n(),
            in_period = sum(between(one_call, min(dates$by_site),
                                    max(dates$by_site))))
misread
```

The single call parses every value and returns no `NA`, and every
disagreement is at Site D. The rows shown are consistent with
`03-FEB-2024` being read as month 03, with `FEB` skipped and `2024`
split into a day, 20, and a two-digit year, 24. Of the
`r misread$n` misread discharge dates, `r misread$in_period` fall
inside the trial's enrollment period, so a range check on discharge
dates catches only `r misread$n - misread$in_period` of them.

### Ambiguous values

Site D's failure comes from a format the orders did not describe
well. Site C's risk is subtler: `03/04/2026` is a valid date under
both `mdy` and `dmy`. `parse_date_time()` chooses an order by
training on the whole vector, so the reading of one value depends on
the order you list and on its neighbors:

```{r}
#| label: types-ambiguous
parse_date_time("03/04/2026", orders = c("mdy", "dmy"))
parse_date_time("03/04/2026", orders = c("dmy", "mdy"))
parse_date_time(c("03/04/2026", "25/04/2026"), orders = c("mdy", "dmy"))
```

Alone, with `mdy` listed first, the value is March 4. Beside a value
that only `dmy` can read, the same value becomes April 3, under the
same call and with no warning. A column's dates can therefore change
when rows are added to it. The defense is to count the values a
second convention would read differently:

```{r}
#| label: types-ambiguous-count
ambiguous <- function(x) {
  as_mdy <- mdy(x, quiet = TRUE)
  as_dmy <- dmy(x, quiet = TRUE)
  !is.na(as_mdy) & !is.na(as_dmy) & as_mdy != as_dmy
}

crf_raw |>
  filter(site == "Site C") |>
  summarize(n = n(), ambiguous = sum(ambiguous(discharge_date)))
```

Only Site C's codebook can resolve those values, which is why the
parse is per site and the order is stated, not guessed.

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**A multi-format parser never says it guessed.** `parse_date_time()`
with several orders returns a date for every value it can read under
any of them. Day-month swaps produce valid dates in the same month
range, and a misread such as Site D's produces a plausible date in
the same year. Parse each source with its single documented order,
and count the ambiguous values before trusting any multi-order
parse.
:::

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
> **Context.** A date column from three sources. Below are twenty
> synthetic values in each source's format, and each source's
> codebook line stating its format.
>
> **Constraints.** Parse each source with its single documented
> order (`ymd()`, `mdy()`, `dmy()`), not `parse_date_time()` with
> several orders and not nested `ifelse()`. Use `quiet = TRUE` and
> count failures explicitly.
>
> **Criteria.** Return a function `parse_source_date(x, source)` and
> a check that reports, per source, the number of `NA`s and the
> number of values that `mdy()` and `dmy()` would read as different
> dates.

*Failure mode.* The model's default answer is `parse_date_time(x,
orders = c("ymd", "mdy", "dmy"))`, often called the robust choice.
It returns a date for every value, so an `NA` count finds nothing,
and it misreads exactly the values this section counts. *Check.*
Compare the model's parse with the per-site parse row by row, as in
`types-dates`; any disagreement is a misread by one of them. Send
synthetic values in the source's format, not real dates of birth
(@sec-ai-governance).
:::

### Excel serial dates

A date column from a spreadsheet may arrive as five-digit numbers,
Excel's count of days from its own origin. Converting with
`as.Date()` counts from R's origin instead:

```{r}
#| label: types-excel-date
as.Date(45405)
as.Date(45405, origin = "1899-12-30")
janitor::excel_numeric_to_date(45405)
```

`as.Date(45405)` is a valid date seventy years from now, and nothing
about it is `NA`.[^excel-origin] Any column whose name says date and
whose values are numbers is a bug until shown otherwise; the
assertion is a range check against the study period.

[^excel-origin]: Since R 4.3.0, `as.Date()` on a number uses
    1970-01-01 as the origin when none is given; earlier versions
    required an `origin`. The Excel origin of 1899-12-30, rather
    than 1900-01-01, absorbs Excel's treatment of 1900 as a leap
    year, which holds for dates after February 1900 in the
    default Windows date system.

### Time zones and daylight saving

HF-HOME records dates without times, which is the safe case for
daily-resolution analyses. Device data, electronic health record
audit logs, and infusion pumps record date-times, and a date-time
without a time zone is ambiguous: Coordinated Universal Time (UTC),
the site's zone, or the zone
of the server that wrote it? `lubridate` parses a date-time without
a zone as UTC; base R uses the session's zone. Say which:

```{r}
#| label: types-timezone
t <- ymd_hms("2026-04-23 14:30:00", tz = "America/Los_Angeles")
t
with_tz(t, "UTC")
force_tz(t, "UTC")
```

`with_tz()` changes the displayed zone without changing the instant;
`force_tz()` changes the instant by declaring that the clock reading
was always in the new zone. Confusing them shifts times by the
offset between the zones, here seven hours.

Daylight-saving transitions add a second trap. In most US time
zones, daylight-saving time began at 2:00 a.m. on March 8, 2026, so
an interval that starts at noon the day before crosses it:

```{r}
#| label: types-dst
start <- ymd_hms("2026-03-07 12:00:00", tz = "America/Los_Angeles")
start + days(1)
start + hours(24)
start + dhours(24)
```

`days(1)` and `hours(24)` are both *periods*: they advance the
clock, and land at noon on March 8. `dhours(24)` is a *duration* of
exactly 86,400 seconds, and lands at 1:00 p.m., because the night of
the transition was only 23 hours long. Use a period for a calendar
notion of a day and a duration for elapsed time, whichever the
analysis requires.

### Exercises

5. Parse `dob` per site and verify it against `demographics.csv`.
   Then parse it with the single `parse_date_time()` call of
   `types-dates`, and count the dates of birth it gets wrong and how
   many of those fall after the patient's discharge date.
6. Count the ambiguous dates of birth at Site C. For one of them,
   show the date `mdy()` and `dmy()` each return.
7. Create a date-time in `America/Los_Angeles` and convert it to UTC
   with `with_tz()` and with `force_tz()`. Explain the difference,
   and say when each is the right call.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-14-5a
dob <- crf_raw |>
  transmute(
    patient_id, site,
    by_site = parse_site_date(dob, site),
    one_call = as_date(parse_date_time(dob,
                                       orders = c("ymd", "mdy", "dmy"),
                                       quiet = TRUE)),
    discharge = parse_site_date(discharge_date, site)
  )
stopifnot(identical(dob$by_site,
                    demographics$dob[match(dob$patient_id,
                                           demographics$patient_id)]))

dob_wrong <- dob |>
  filter(by_site != one_call) |>
  summarize(wrong = n(), after_discharge = sum(one_call > discharge),
            .by = site)
dob_wrong
```

The per-site parse agrees with the answer key for every patient. The
single call misreads only Site D's dates of birth. Of its
`r dob_wrong$wrong` misreads, `r dob_wrong$after_discharge` place
the birth after the discharge, which a range check catches; the
other `r dob_wrong$wrong - dob_wrong$after_discharge` are plausible
ages and are caught by nothing but the comparison.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-14-6
site_c_dob <- crf_raw |> filter(site == "Site C") |> pull(dob)
sum(ambiguous(site_c_dob))
example <- site_c_dob[ambiguous(site_c_dob)][1]
c(raw = example, mdy = format(mdy(example)),
  dmy = format(dmy(example)))
```

Site C's codebook says `MM/DD/YYYY`, so `mdy()` is right. Nothing in
the values says so: for each ambiguous date, both readings are real
dates.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-14-5
t <- ymd_hms("2026-04-23 14:30:00", tz = "America/Los_Angeles")

with_tz(t, "UTC")
force_tz(t, "UTC")
```

`with_tz` preserves the moment and relabels it; `force_tz` preserves
the digits and moves the moment. Use `with_tz` when combining data
recorded in different zones, and `force_tz` only to repair a
timestamp that was stamped with the wrong zone to begin with.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Three things go wrong with dates in this chapter: a
multi-format column parsed with one `parse_date_time()` call, an
Excel serial number read with `as.Date()`, and `days(1)` used where
a duration was meant. Which will your code tell you about?

**Answer.** None of them. The single parse returns a date for every
Site D value and is wrong for some; an `NA` count finds nothing. The
Excel number becomes a valid date seventy years out. The daylight
saving case returns a correct answer to a different question:
`days(1)` gives the same clock time the next day, `dhours(24)` the
instant 24 hours later, and R cannot know which you meant. A bug
that produces `NA` is cheap; a bug that produces a plausible date is
expensive, and the comparison against a per-source parse or a range
check is the assertion that makes it loud (Habit 8).
:::

## Worked example: a typed patient table {#sec-types-worked}

The script below gathers the chapter into one patient-level table:
site and sex as factors with declared levels, the discharge date
parsed per site, the arm with its reference set, and three
medication summaries. It reuses `crf_typed`, `parse_site_date()`,
and the parsed `meds` from the sections above.

```{r}
#| label: types-worked-example
med_summary <- meds |>
  summarize(
    n_meds    = n(),
    on_sglt2  = any(drug_class == "SGLT2 inhibitor", na.rm = TRUE),
    on_arni   = any(drug_class == "ARNI", na.rm = TRUE),
    loop_mg_day = sum(
      if_else(str_detect(med_text, regex("furosemide|lasix",
                                         ignore_case = TRUE)),
              dose_mg * per_day, 0)
    ),
    .by = patient_id
  )

patients <- crf_typed |>
  transmute(
    patient_id, site, sex,
    discharge_date = parse_site_date(discharge_date,
                                     as.character(site))
  ) |>
  left_join(randomization |> select(patient_id, arm),
            by = "patient_id", relationship = "one-to-one",
            unmatched = "error") |>
  left_join(med_summary, by = "patient_id",
            relationship = "one-to-one") |>
  mutate(
    arm = factor(arm, levels = c("Usual care", "Home health")),
    across(c(n_meds, loop_mg_day), \(x) coalesce(x, 0)),
    across(c(on_sglt2, on_arni), \(x) coalesce(x, FALSE))
  )

glimpse(patients)
patients |>
  summarize(n = n(), sglt2 = mean(on_sglt2), arni = mean(on_arni),
            furosemide = mean(loop_mg_day > 0), .by = arm) |>
  arrange(arm)
```

Two judgments are written into the code. Patients with no
medication rows get `n_meds = 0` and `FALSE` flags, which is the
codebook's meaning of an absent row; in a file where absence could
mean 'not recorded', the right value would be `NA`. And
`loop_mg_day` counts furosemide only, because torsemide is about
twice as potent per milligram and adding the two would mix units of
effect; a dose-equivalence rule belongs in the analysis plan, not
in a cleaning script's arithmetic.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Confirm the types and levels, and check the medication count against
the clean `baseline.csv`, which records each patient's number of
discharge medications:

```{r}
#| label: types-worked-verify
baseline <- read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, "baseline.csv"),
                     col_types = cols(patient_id = col_character()),
                     show_col_types = FALSE)

stopifnot(
  nrow(patients) == nrow(randomization),
  identical(levels(patients$arm), c("Usual care", "Home health")),
  identical(levels(patients$site), site_levels),
  inherits(patients$discharge_date, "Date"),
  !anyNA(patients$discharge_date),
  all(patients$n_meds ==
        baseline$discharge_med_count[match(patients$patient_id,
                                           baseline$patient_id)])
)
sum(patients$n_meds == 0)
```

The last assertion checks the string work end to end: a patient
whose medication rows were lost or duplicated would fail it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** The worked example converts `arm` to a factor at the
end of the script, after both joins. Why not at the start, when
`randomization.csv` is read?

**Answer.** Here the arm is not a join key, so converting early
would do no harm; the reason is where the declaration sits.
Converting at the end keeps every column that a join, filter, or
recode touches in its plain type, and puts the reference level
beside the analysis that depends on it, where a reviewer looks for
it. Had `arm` been a key, or been recoded after the read, an early
factor would have needed its levels managed at every step, and a
join would have given it the union of two level sets.
:::

## Rules of thumb

1. **Habit 7: convert late, validate early.** Keep categories as
   character until the model, then declare the levels and the
   reference in writing, and assert them.
2. **Habit 8: a parser that always returns a value cannot tell you
   it guessed.** A first-number regex, a multi-order date parse,
   and an Excel serial date all produce plausible values; compare
   against a second, stricter reading and count the disagreements.
3. **Habit 12: every model output is a hypothesis until verified.**
   A model's regular expression or date parser is checked on the
   full column, with a cross-tabulation of what it matched.

## Cumulative practice

8. *Cumulative (uses @sec-joins).* Add each patient's discharge
   potassium from `labs.csv` (visit `-01`, test `K`) to `patients`,
   with a declared relationship, after handling the duplicated
   discharge potassium that @sec-wrangling found. Flag the patients
   discharged on a potassium supplement (`K-Dur`, `KCl`, or
   `potassium chloride`, in any case) and compare their median
   discharge potassium with everyone else's.
9. *On your own work (no key).* Write a function that takes any
   character column and returns each value with its count and
   proportion, and use it to audit the categorical variables in a
   recent analysis of yours. Report every level you did not expect.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution to exercise 8'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-14-8
labs <- read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, "labs.csv"),
                 col_types = cols(patient_id = col_character()),
                 show_col_types = FALSE)
discharge_k <- labs |>
  filter(str_ends(visit_id, "-01"), test_code == "K") |>
  distinct() |>
  filter(n() == 1, .by = patient_id) |>
  select(patient_id, k_discharge = value)

k_supplement <- meds |>
  filter(str_detect(med_text, regex("k-dur|\\bkcl\\b|potassium chloride",
                                    ignore_case = TRUE))) |>
  distinct(patient_id) |>
  mutate(on_k = TRUE)

with_k <- patients |>
  left_join(discharge_k, by = "patient_id",
            relationship = "one-to-one") |>
  left_join(k_supplement, by = "patient_id",
            relationship = "one-to-one") |>
  mutate(on_k = coalesce(on_k, FALSE))

stopifnot(nrow(with_k) == nrow(patients))
with_k |>
  summarize(n = n(), missing_k = sum(is.na(k_discharge)),
            median_k = median(k_discharge, na.rm = TRUE), .by = on_k)
```

`distinct()` removes the exact duplicate, and the `n() == 1` filter
sets aside the potassium that was re-run with a different value, as
@sec-wrangling did, so that patient's potassium is missing rather
than invented; the `missing_k` column shows it. The orphan patient
in `labs.csv` never reaches `patients`, because the left join keeps
only randomized patients. Whether supplemented patients differ is
descriptive here; potassium supplements are prescribed in response
to low potassium, so any difference is confounded by indication.
:::

## Cheat sheet

| Task | Code | Guards against |
|---|---|---|
| Collapse spellings to levels | `fct_collapse(x, F = c("F", "f", "2"), M = c(...))` | Several codes for one category |
| Rename levels | `fct_recode(x, Female = "F")` | Codes in tables and figures |
| Declare the level set | `factor(x, levels = site_levels)` | Variant spellings becoming categories |
| Set the reference | `fct_relevel(arm, "Usual care")` | Effects reported in the wrong direction |
| Order by frequency or value | `fct_infreq(x)`, `fct_reorder(x, y, median)` | Alphabetical order in plots |
| Lump rare levels | `fct_lump_min(x, min = 10)` | Unstable estimates for tiny groups |
| Count levels, including empty | `fct_count(x)` | Dropped or unexpected levels |
| Detect, ignoring case | `str_detect(x, regex("lasix", ignore_case = TRUE))` | Undercounts from capitalization |
| Capture parts | `str_match(x, "(\\d+(?:\\.\\d+)?)\\s*(mg\|mcg)")` | First-number parsing |
| Normalize text | `str_to_lower()`, `str_squish()`, `str_remove_all(x, "\\.")` | Spellings that differ only in form |
| Parse one known format | `ymd()`, `mdy()`, `dmy()` | Guessed conventions |
| Find ambiguous dates | `!is.na(mdy(x)) & !is.na(dmy(x)) & mdy(x) != dmy(x)` | Silent day-month swaps |
| Excel serial dates | `janitor::excel_numeric_to_date(x)` | Dates seventy years off |
| Change displayed zone | `with_tz(t, "UTC")` | Mixing zones across sources |
| Repair a wrong zone | `force_tz(t, "UTC")` | Timestamps stamped in the wrong zone |
| Calendar day versus elapsed time | `days(1)` versus `ddays(1)` | One-hour errors at daylight-saving transitions |
| Add months safely | `d %m+% months(3)` | Invalid dates such as February 30 |

: Factors, strings, and dates at a glance. {#tbl-types-cheat-sheet}

  expressions, factors, and dates and times.

## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-14}

1. Before R 4.0, `read.csv()` and `data.frame()` converted
   character columns to factors by default. Levels appeared where a
   character string was expected, for example as merge keys, new
   values could not be assigned without first adding a level, and
   `as.numeric()` on a numeric-looking column returned codes rather
   than values. R 4.0 made `FALSE` the default, and the old default
   now matters only when reading older code.
2. `str_detect(string, pattern)` returns a logical vector of the
   same length as `string`: `TRUE` where the pattern matched,
   `FALSE` elsewhere. `str_extract()` returns a character vector,
   the first matching substring per input, or `NA` where there was
   no match. `str_detect()` is for filtering and flagging;
   `str_extract()` is for pulling out parts.
3. `parse_date_time(x, orders = c('ymd', 'mdy', 'Bdy'))` parses all
   three. A fourth value `'03/04/2026'` is valid as March 4 and as
   April 3. With only `mdy` among the slash orders it is read as
   March 4, but if `dmy` were also listed, the reading would depend
   on the order of the list and on the other values in the vector,
   with no warning. Parse each source with its single documented
   order, and count the values that a second convention would read
   differently.
